key_features.classic_presentation: Acute gastroenteritis presents with DIARRHEA as the PREDOMINANT symptom (often more prominent than pain), with 3+ loose or watery stools per day. Abdominal pain is CRAMPY, DIFFUSE, and INTERMITTENT (comes and goes in waves) - NOT constant or localized to one spot. Pain is typically 3-6/10 severity, relieved temporarily after bowel movements. Onset is sudden, usually within hours to 1-2 days. Key associated symptoms: NAUSEA AND VOMITING often occur BEFORE or SIMULTANEOUSLY with diarrhea (unlike appendicitis where pain comes first), low-grade fever or no fever (high fever suggests invasive bacteria), and diffuse abdominal cramping with bowel movements. Location: Pain is periumbilical or diffuse throughout abdomen, NOT localized to one quadrant. Key history: Recent sick contacts, contaminated food/water, travel, daycare exposure. APPETITE is often PRESERVED or only mildly reduced (unlike appendicitis where anorexia is severe). Key positives: Hyperactive bowel sounds, diffuse tenderness without guarding, watery or bloody diarrhea. Key negatives: Pain that MIGRATES to RLQ suggests appendicitis not gastroenteritis. SEVERE localized tenderness with guarding rules out simple gastroenteritis. Pain without diarrhea is uncommon.

red_flags: Severe dehydration (dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output, orthostatic hypotension) - needs IV fluids
Bloody diarrhea with high fever >102°F - invasive bacterial infection (Shigella, Salmonella, E. coli), may need antibiotics
Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs - suggests perforation or alternative diagnosis, not simple gastroenteritis
Immunocompromised patients or infants - higher risk of severe dehydration and complications
